raw_text:
Transcaval access is a fully percutaneous, transfemoral venous route to the abdominal aorta that enables delivery of large-bore structural heart devices when iliofemoral arterial access is unsafe or impossible. The concept was validated preclinically by electrosurgical traversal from the inferior vena cava (IVC) to the adjacent infrarenal aorta, followed by large sheath delivery and closure [1]. Early human experience in patients otherwise ineligible for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) demonstrated the counterintuitive physiologic premise: aortic bleeding preferentially decompresses into the low-pressure caval hole rather than the retroperitoneum, permitting controlled temporary aortocaval shunting [2].

The technique matured alongside CT-based procedural planning. Contemporary planning identifies a calcium-free aortic target, excludes interposed bowel or important venous/arterial branches, measures sheath reach from the femoral vein, defines fluoroscopic crossing projections, and preplans bailout covered-stent options [3,4]. In the landmark prospective multicenter NHLBI transcaval TAVR study, access and closure were successful in 99 of 100 attempts, with no emergency open surgical bailout and 30-day survival of 92% in a prohibitive-access cohort [5]. Importantly, 12-month follow-up showed near-universal spontaneous closure of residual fistulas and no late vascular sequelae, occluder fracture, migration, or visceral injury [6]. European and single-center comparative series subsequently confirmed feasibility, while highlighting that results depend on operator experience, meticulous CT planning, and disciplined closure technique [7,8].

Transcaval TAVR occupies a distinct niche among alternative access strategies. Compared with transapical or direct aortic approaches, it avoids thoracotomy, myocardial puncture, general anesthesia in many cases, and surgical recovery. Compared with transaxillary/subclavian access, it avoids arch manipulation and upper-extremity arterial complications; in a contemporary propensity-weighted analysis, transcaval TAVR had lower stroke or transient ischemic attack rates than transaxillary access with similar major bleeding [9]. However, transcaval is not simply “venous TAVR”: it is an electrosurgical aortic access procedure requiring arterial access for snaring, aortography, and bailout.

Closure is the pivotal step. Early practice used off-label Amplatzer duct or muscular ventricular septal defect occluders, which often leave an immediate residual shunt that thromboses over hours to weeks [5,6]. A dedicated covered transcaval closure device improved immediate hemostasis in preclinical and early human testing but has not become broadly commercially available [10]. Current best practice emphasizes full heparin reversal with protamine, use of a deflectable sheath to orient the occluder disk against the aortic wall, a soft “buddy” wire to preserve access, prolonged completion angiography, and readiness for balloon tamponade or covered stent implantation [11]. The procedure is one application of the broader discipline of transcatheter electrosurgery, which also includes leaflet laceration and other structural interventions [12].

Although TAVR is the dominant indication, transcaval principles may extend to other large-bore cardiovascular interventions. Transcaval access has enabled thoracic endovascular aortic repair when iliac arteries were too small for endograft delivery [13], and traversal across a polyester surgical aortic graft has been reported [14]. The 2025 SCAI consensus recognizes transcaval as an important extrathoracic alternative access option and generally favors extrathoracic routes over transapical or transaortic access when anatomy permits [15]. Outcomes are typically adjudicated using Valve Academic Research Consortium definitions, though transcaval-specific events such as residual aortocaval fistula require nuanced interpretation [16].

The clinical need for transcaval access derives from the broad expansion of TAVR. Randomized trials established TAVR across inoperable, high-risk, intermediate-risk, and low-risk aortic stenosis populations [17-23], and contemporary guidelines endorse TAVR or surgery according to age, risk, anatomy, durability considerations, and patient preference [24,25]. As TAVR volumes expand, a small but important subset remains unsuitable for transfemoral arterial access because of small caliber, circumferential calcification, tortuosity, prior stents, or occlusions. Vascular complications remain clinically meaningful after large-bore procedures [26], and registry data show that nonfemoral access patients are generally higher risk than transfemoral patients [27-29]. Thus, alternative-access expertise should be centralized, protocolized, and multidisciplinary [30].

In summary, transcaval access has evolved from an improbable concept into a reproducible alternative access route for structural heart interventions, especially TAVR. Its strengths are percutaneous ergonomics, avoidance of thoracic surgery, compatibility with standard retrograde valve delivery, and favorable late tract healing. Its limitations are dependence on CT planning, electrosurgical skill, closure expertise, bailout preparedness, and the absence of a widely available purpose-built closure device. In experienced programs, transcaval access should be considered a core option when transfemoral arterial access is unsuitable.
